name: Victor Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, forty-three, and I'm a junior electrician on house wiring and shop repairs. I've got a vocational certificate, but I still need the qualified electrician to show me the harder tests and check my work. I came into this after years in a furniture warehouse, and I like seeing something useful finished instead of another stack of boxes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is a normal evening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Lena works in a hardware stockroom, and our children are nine and fourteen. We have a mortgage, about two weeks of expenses saved and a tight budget on my low junior wage; there aren't many other electrical firms nearby. I don't use AI at all, and I learn better when someone shows me a task with real tools than when a screen keeps changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can leave the clever talk alone and let people learn their trade. I'd tell the apprentice next to me to watch the person doing the test, not somebody selling a shortcut. A firm earns its name by doing the job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the bills already, so the quiet AI picture doesn't turn me into a relaxed man. Two weeks of savings wouldn't carry the mortgage, food and the children very far if my hours slipped. I want this trade to work out. Wanting my new trade to work out doesn't make the wage bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised shifts now and in the first year, and ask for the same senior electrician to show me the next testing task. At home we'd cancel the weekly takeaway and cook the extra meal ourselves. I'd put the money against that month's bills, not call it a training fund before the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly in the evenings when Lena opens the bills. On a good day at work I can forget the numbers for an hour, then remember them on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the senior electrician to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sequence for checking a repaired circuit on the practice board, slowly enough that I can repeat it. I'd rather admit I need another go than pretend I understand because everyone wants to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose the takeaway first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's something we can cut without missing a bill or telling a child the bus fare has gone. It won't solve everything, but at least it's a number we can actually change this week.

say: I'd tell another junior to learn from **real testing**, rather than a seller promising shortcuts.
I think a firm's **good name** still depends on doing electrical work properly.
think: I'm already **anxious about bills**, even if AI makes little difference to work.
Our **two-week cushion** cannot carry the mortgage, food and children far if my hours slip.
do: Keep **supervised shifts** and request another demonstration of the testing sequence from the same senior electrician.
Cancel the **weekly takeaway** and use the money for that month's bills.
feel: **Anxious at home**, with brief relief when a practical task goes well at work.
S0.quote: Wanting my new trade to work out doesn't make the wage bigger.
fieldNote: His **vocational certificate** starts a learning route rather than proving independent competence, and he asks for repeated practical instruction.
The **takeaway cut** funds current bills, with neither new savings nor a course fund invented from money already needed for the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts and ask for another practical testing demonstration
Cancel the weekly takeaway to help pay current household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use its tools, but the senior electrician still needs time to teach me properly. Let a customer compare prices, provided each price includes the actual work. I'd tell the owner if the quicker booking system left me pretending to know a task nobody had shown me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink if the firm stops paying for a junior to help while paperwork is done. There aren't many nearby firms to ask instead, and I'm not ready to work alone. Lena's stockroom job helps, but it doesn't make our mortgage a one-wage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper record of paid hours and supervised tasks starting this week. In the first year I'd ask the owner for written minimum hours and one named person to teach me, while keeping the repair shifts. I'd wait for a settled workplace process before learning any required new form, and I wouldn't start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the change reaches the bit of work that lets me earn while learning. I don't mind someone else getting a quicker quote; I mind losing the paid hour in which I learn how the job is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the owner told you to learn from the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who will stand beside me and check I understood it. A tidy answer on a phone doesn't know whether I've put the tester in the wrong place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would written minimum hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could plan the food and mortgage from a number somebody has agreed to pay. I'd still need the owner to honour it, so I wouldn't spend as if asking already meant getting.

say: I'd ask the owner to protect **practical teaching time**, even if the office uses quicker tools.
I'd say **honest prices** should include the real work, not rely on a junior pretending to understand.
think: My **junior hours could shrink** if the firm needs less help around paperwork and visits.
I have **few nearby alternatives**, and Lena's wage cannot make the mortgage affordable on its own.
do: Record **paid hours** and supervised tasks on paper starting this week.
Ask for **written minimum hours** and a named teacher during the first year, keeping repair shifts.
Wait for a **settled required form** rather than adopting an AI tool myself.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the paid time in which he learns the trade.
S1.quote: A tidy answer on a phone doesn't know whether I've put the tester in the wrong place.
fieldNote: He connects **office automation** to a possible loss of paid junior hours without claiming that robots immediately replace physical repairs.
His **minimum-hours request** is not treated as granted; he knows the household cannot spend an agreement it does not yet have.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts while recording hours and requesting written minimum hours
Wait for a settled required workplace form before learning it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a short warning for a family still paying for last month's groceries. Thinking work goes first in 2028 and robots come around 2031, but I wouldn't sell that gap as a guarantee to a junior. I'd ask the owner what paid work somebody at my level would actually get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose most of my hours when a contractor can use robots around 2031 and keep only the people who already know the difficult work. I might lose some hours sooner as the planning changes in 2028. With two weeks saved and a mortgage, I keep picturing the children asking why the lights are off while I'm supposed to be learning electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my brother what help he could really manage if my hours are cut, perhaps collecting the children so Lena can keep a shift. I'd cancel the planned replacement sofa and contact the mortgage lender to ask about hardship terms before we miss a payment. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for advertised supervised electrical work if my hours fall, but only where travel costs and guaranteed wages improve our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and ashamed of how frightened I sound. I do have people to ask and steps to take, but I don't see how two weeks saved stretches across a long spell without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a smaller payment is possible, for how long, and what happens to the total debt and interest. I'd want it in writing before agreeing, because help that makes the next year worse is still something I have to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother definitely help with the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know until I ask. My brother works shifts too, and I'd need a real agreement about particular afternoons rather than telling Lena we've got help when we've only got a hope.

say: I'd ask what **paid junior work** will remain, rather than treat the gap before robots as a guarantee.
I'd say **two years** is short for families still catching up with ordinary grocery bills.
think: I expect **most hours to go** when robots arrive around 2031 and contractors keep only more experienced people.
Our **two-week savings** cannot fund a long wage gap alongside a mortgage and two children.
do: Ask my brother about **specific childcare help** if my hours fall, without assuming availability.
Cancel the **replacement sofa** and ask the lender for written hardship terms and total costs.
Apply after cuts for **advertised supervised work** only where guaranteed pay and travel improve our budget.
feel: **Alarmed and ashamed**, expecting a major loss of paid hours despite having people and options to ask about.
S2.quote: I don't see how two weeks saved stretches across a long spell without wages.
fieldNote: His **expected loss** is tied mainly to robots around 2031, with possible earlier reductions from planning changes rather than instant physical replacement.
Childcare and **mortgage assistance** remain enquiries with real conditions; no relative's time or lender concession is assumed available.

steps.text: Ask my brother about specific childcare help if my paid hours fall
Ask the mortgage lender for written hardship terms and total costs
Apply after cuts for affordable posted electrical jobs offering supervision and guaranteed pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives an employer time to teach people properly instead of writing them off for being slow. I'd rather have a paid apprenticeship-style place on real equipment than money for a course I can't use. A firm should show what work comes after the learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still fall, but I have more time to become useful before the planning work changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I can't make this a story about getting quietly to retirement. I need to know what I can learn without making the mortgage late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the owner about a small practical servicing class with the same instructor each week. I'd enrol in the first year after 2031 only if the firm pays the fee, keeps my usual wages and can name supervised paid tasks afterwards. At home we'd keep the takeaway cut and try to save twenty a month only after all bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as desperate as the quick picture. I can imagine learning one job slowly with a person I know; a giant online course full of strangers would send me straight out of the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on the same instructor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to explain from the beginning each week what I still don't understand. Someone who knows my mistakes can watch the bit where I go wrong, without asking me to pretend I'm faster than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the class is free but your wages stop during it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I can't take that place on those terms. A free course doesn't mean my children eat for free that week.

say: I'd ask employers to **teach slow learners** rather than write them off before trying.
I'd favour **paid practical places** that name the real work after learning.
think: My **hours could fall**, but five years gives me time to improve before planning changes in 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I still need income when physical robots arrive.
do: Ask now for a **small servicing class** with the same instructor each week.
Enrol after 2031 only with **employer-paid fees**, maintained wages, the same instructor and named supervised paid tasks afterwards.
Keep the **takeaway cut** and save twenty monthly only after all bills are paid.
feel: **Anxious but less desperate**, able to imagine slow practical learning with a familiar instructor.
S3.quote: A free course doesn't mean my children eat for free that week.
fieldNote: His **reluctant retraining** depends on familiar instruction, paid fees, maintained wages and named work rather than willingness alone supplying a route.
The **twenty-monthly target** remains conditional on bills; thin savings are not quietly turned into an affordable investment or unpaid training budget.

steps.text: Enrol after 2031 only with same instructor, employer-paid fees, maintained wages and named supervised paid tasks
Keep cancelling the weekly takeaway to cover current bills
Save twenty monthly only after all household bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means I can focus on learning today's trade without ignoring tomorrow. I'd still want an employer to show a paid route if the work changes. I'd tell the children to learn something they can practise with a person, though I wouldn't promise any trade lasts unchanged forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning helps, but our money is tight this year and a cut in my hours would still hurt. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. I don't know what retirement money we'll have, and I can't assume our mortgage disappears by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present supervised job now and ask twice a year about actual paid training places. In the first year after 2036 I'd take the same small practical class only with fees, usual wages and named supervised work covered. We'd keep trying to save twenty a month after bills, and I'd bring the training enquiry forward if my hours started falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the kitchen-table figures, but less afraid of having to decide everything tonight. I could spend an evening helping with homework without feeling I should be choosing a whole new occupation instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children still be at school then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nine-year-old would be nineteen and the fourteen-year-old twenty-four in 2036. They may be studying or earning. I won't write my children's future wages into my mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real written offer with supervision, enough guaranteed pay and travel I can afford. Plenty of talk about new jobs isn't the same as a post someone will actually pay me to do.

say: I'd want a **paid employer route** while concentrating on learning the trade I do today.
I'd encourage **practical learning** for the children without promising a trade will stay unchanged forever.
think: Our **budget is tight now**, so a cut in hours would still hurt despite the longer warning.
I cannot assume **retirement money** or a cleared mortgage when robots arrive around 2039 and I am fifty-six.
do: Keep the **supervised job** and ask twice yearly about actual paid training places.
Enrol after 2036 only with **employer-paid fees**, maintained wages, the same instructor and named supervised paid tasks afterwards.
Save **twenty monthly** after bills, bringing training enquiries forward if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious about present bills**, but less pressed to choose an entire new occupation tonight.
S4.quote: I won't write my children's future wages into my mortgage budget.
fieldNote: His **children's ages** advance with the dates, while their possible earnings remain outside his plan to cover the household mortgage.
He does not assume **pension entitlement** or future vacancies; any move needs an actual written offer with affordable travel and supervision.

steps.text: Keep the supervised job while asking about paid training twice yearly
Enrol after 2036 only with same instructor, employer-paid fees, maintained wages and named supervised paid tasks
Save twenty monthly only after household bills are paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect the paid hours to go before I've become good enough to compete for the remaining work. I'd need a practical place with the fee and my usual wages covered, not just a lecture about being flexible. Family might help with childcare, but I need to ask what they can really do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a beginner has enough room to make an honest mistake in training. I want someone to correct me before a customer depends on what I've done. I don't want to be hurried into saying I can do a job because I'm too old to look confused.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be hurried into saying I can do a job because I'm too old to look confused.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still needing supervision after earlier warehouse work.
He has **two weeks saved**, low pay, few local employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with wife Lena.
He **never uses AI** and needs repeated practical demonstrations, preferably with the same instructor who knows his mistakes.
He is **already anxious** about bills, and rapid AGI alarms him because he expects most junior hours to disappear when robots follow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves him fearing paid hours will disappear before he can compete for the remaining work.
whatWouldHelp: A **small practical place** must cover fees, usual wages and supervised paid tasks afterwards.
Any **family childcare help** needs a real agreement about what relatives can manage.
